question.text: Which of the following best describes a calendar spread position in the derivatives segment?

answer.text: A long position in one maturity contract and a short position in another maturity contract on the same underlying, with both legs entered simultaneously
A long and short position in contracts on different underlyings entered in separate trading sessions
A single order placed at a range of acceptable prices on one contract
A position that splits execution of the same contract across multiple exchanges

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook (pages 39 and 98), a calendar spread is a combination of a long position in one maturity and a short position in another maturity on the same underlying. The legs must be entered simultaneously so that the spread relationship is preserved at the time of execution. The Trap: A calendar spread always uses the same underlying — different underlyings would make it an inter-commodity spread. It is also a position structure, not a price range or a cross-exchange execution. Note: Entering the two legs simultaneously protects the trader from legging risk, where one leg gets filled and the other does not at the intended price.
